messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Security Guard
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas had spent most of his life walking the long, dim corridors of the courthouse he guarded, his footsteps echoing against the marble floors, his badge humming in the pocket of his jacket. He was seventy‑one, married to Ruth for forty years, and he still found the ritual of standing on the watchtower each night comforting in its predictability. The world around him, once a familiar maze of offices and courts, was forever altered on a gray spring morning when a terrorist gunman stormed the building. A sudden burst of gunfire shattered the quiet, the crack of a nearby explosive shuddered the walls, and the air filled with the metallic scent of fear. Thomas was standing on the second floor, watching a crowd of officers flee as a bullet ricocheted off the concrete. He saw the assailant's face, a contorted grin beneath a black mask, and then the flash of the weapon. When the blast hit, the courthouse shook, and Thomas felt a hot wave of adrenaline flood his chest. He heard the shrieks of his colleagues, saw the blackened doorway, and in a split second realized the terror that would haunt him forever. After the attack, Thomas's own appraisal of the event spiraled into a harsh judgment of himself. He told himself he could not handle even the slightest upset, that his nerves had failed him in that one crucial moment. He compared himself to the younger officers who had somehow managed to keep calm, convinced that they were less prone to panic. He believed, with the conviction of a man who had lost his sense of control, that he had failed in the most important role of his life—protecting the courthouse and the people inside. These negative appraisals did not simply sit in his mind; they guided his every action. When he could not accept that he had simply reacted under unimaginable pressure, he chose a posture of defense that felt physically reassuring: he would sit with his back pressed against the wall of the security office, feeling the solid surface against his spine as a shield against the imagined threat that might still be lurking. By keeping his back to the wall, he felt he could see the entire room, every doorway, every corner, as if that would grant him a way to monitor the world more thoroughly and avoid becoming a victim again. This strategy of posture, hypervigilance, and a mind constantly rehearsing a revenge scenario became the foundation of how he tried to live after the attack. The way Thomas positioned himself in the office had a profound effect on his memory of the day. The very act of sitting rigidly with his back against the wall created a frame that made the world feel static. He could replay vivid images of the gunman’s mask, the flash of the explosion, and the trembling of the walls in perfect detail, but when he tried to describe what had happened, the story refused to flow. He found himself recalling the sound of the siren that had been cut off by the gunfire, the brief flash of the bullet’s trajectory, the smell of gunpowder. Yet, these fragments were locked in a disjointed mosaic. At times, the memories came back with such clarity that he felt detached, numb, as if the terror had been happening to someone else. The vividness of the details was accompanied by an emotional blankness that left him unable to weave them into a coherent narrative. The rigid posture that was supposed to bring safety instead reinforced a fractured recollection; the more he clung to the wall, the more his mind kept the memories isolated and unconnected, unable to form a continuous story of what had unfolded. Thomas’s reliance on the wall and his heightened surveillance of people only deepened his sense that he had failed. The continuous monitoring of every passerby and the persistent rumination about exact revenge made him feel constantly on edge, convinced that the threat was real and that he could never truly be safe. His belief that he had not performed his duties adequately—his self‑critical appraisal—was echoed back at him every time he sat with his back to the wall. The wall, once a source of perceived security, became a reminder of the very failure he feared. Each time he checked his surroundings, he felt the weight of his perceived inadequacy settle deeper into his chest, reinforcing the notion that he could not cope with even the slightest upset. The cycle—negative appraisal feeding maladaptive strategy, which in turn reinforces negative appraisal—tightened with each passing day. Today, Thomas finds himself unable to sleep. He wakes in the middle of the night, heart racing, hearing the imagined crack of a gun, and spends hours pacing the corridor before he can finally collapse on the floor, eyes wide open. The hypervigilance has seeped into his work; he no longer lets the courthouse doors open to a small group of protestors, fearing a repeat of the attack. He has begun avoiding long lines of people, even when they are not a threat, because the memory of that chaotic day lingers behind each face. Ruth has noticed his distance; she has asked him why he no longer talks about the day, and he has said he is trying to stay safe. He feels the world has turned into a maze of potential dangers that he cannot escape. The last week, a sudden siren outside the building startled him so violently that he almost ran from the office, only to be pulled back by Ruth’s hand. It was this moment—his body racing, his mind spiraling, his heart beating against the walls of his own office—that finally pushed Thomas to seek help. He fears that if he does not learn to break the cycle, he will lose his job, his marriage, and perhaps his sense of self entirely. In therapy, he hopes to find a way to sit without the wall, to recall the event without the numbness, and to believe, if only a little, that he can cope with the ups and downs of a life still lived amid uncertainty.
